title: A Poem on God's Most Beautiful Names
intro: In his preface Muhammad Taqi al-Din al-Hilali dates the poem to 10 Dhu al-Qa'da 1397 AH (1977 CE). Having read two poems that grouped several divine names in a verse, he wanted room beside each name for a prayer that someone could learn by heart. Bandar al-Abdali, who wrote a commentary on the poem, distinguishes the hadith about ninety-nine names from the list in one version, which he attributes to its transmitters. After five opening verses he asks in turn for such things as insight after the loss of his sight, a livelihood, or judgement in a dispute. At the close he returns to the blessing on the Prophet and his family.

translation: I begin in the name of God, the One without beginning,
whose bounty, generosity and goodness have always been.
1.sharh: The opening sets one beginning against eternity. The poet is just starting his work, while the generosity of the One he names has always been there.

translation: Then blessings upon Muhammad and upon
the Prophet's family, to whom honour and welcome are due.
2.sharh: The second half completes a blessing left open at the break. Its word for welcome originally means what a host sets before an honoured guest.

translation: The most beautiful names belong to God. In anyone who invokes him
by them in sincerity, goodness is plain to see.
3.sharh: The names lead to an act. The line echoes the Quranic invitation to call on God by them and asks what such an invocation reveals about a sincere petitioner.

translation: I set them in verse, seeking God's face through them,
to ease their learning for those who pray, and for me.
4.sharh: The writer includes himself among his pupils. Verse gives the person who wants to pray something to remember, and composing it is itself an act of devotion.

translation: So I began, asking God for help with
what I had set out to do, and success in doing it.
5.sharh: Even the making of the poem needs a prayer. The little word “with” carries the first half across the break to the undertaking for which he asks help.

translation: From God I hope for ease without delay
and for my Lord to deliver me from fear.
6.sharh: The first petition distinguishes the trouble from the fear it causes. He hopes for circumstances to ease quickly and for his own inward alarm to lift.

translation: You are our All-Merciful in this life and the next.
By your grace, have mercy on my weakness and grant my hope.
7.sharh: Calling God “our” Merciful One takes in both worlds and a whole community. The voice then comes down to one person's weakness and one unspoken hope.

translation: Merciful to all believers, answer
the prayer of a weak servant who persists in error.
8.sharh: This time mercy is invoked for believers, including someone who keeps doing wrong. His persistence makes the plea different from a request on grounds of weakness alone.

translation: Master, your servant in distress pleads
with you. I have no one else to cure my ills.
9.sharh: The relationship of master and servant first explains whom he can turn to. Only at the end does he name what has driven him there, the ills he longs to have cured.

translation: Most Holy, cleanse my heart so I may follow
guidance and always be occupied with remembering you, my Lord.
10.sharh: He asks what holiness might mean for the life of a human heart. Once cleansed, that heart would have a continuing occupation in the remembrance of God.

translation: Source of peace, may safety go with me
from every evil, every fault and every foolish word.
11.sharh: The divine name Salam unfolds into several kinds of safety. The last danger can come from the speaker's own tongue, since khatal includes foolish speech.

translation: Giver of security, grant me safety and well-being
throughout my life and on the day of terror and shame.
12.sharh: Here the name means the One who gives security. He wants its protection throughout an ordinary lifetime and also on the day when his own deeds will be exposed.

translation: Watchful Guardian, keep all of us always safe
from fears in every particular and as a whole.
13.sharh: The prayer widens from one person's safety to that of everyone with him. It leaves room even for dangers they can name only in general.

translation: Mighty One, great might is yours. Grant us
honour that continues into all the ages.
14.sharh: Might belongs to God in the first half. In human hands honour has to be given, and the speaker asks that time should never wear that gift away.

translation: Mighty Restorer, I am broken. You mend me.
Break my enemies, morning and evening.
15.sharh: The Arabic name allows both overwhelming power and the mending of something broken. What he begs for himself is the exact reverse of what he wishes on his enemies.

translation: Our God is supreme in greatness. We magnify him.
Bring anyone who grows arrogant down to the depths.
16.sharh: One Arabic root does double duty. In God it names greatness worthy of reverence, while in a human being it becomes the arrogance for which the speaker asks a fall.

translation: Creator of all creatures, always grant me their good
and keep from me the harm of the cunning schemer.
17.sharh: Having placed all creatures together under their Creator, he distinguishes what they can bring him. He hopes to receive their good and be spared the harm concealed in another person's designs.

translation: Originator, grant me a speedy recovery from you,
and clothe my body in its ample robes.
18.sharh: The words for the Originator and for recovery share a sound. Health becomes a set of ample clothes reaching every part of the body that needs it.

translation: Fashioner, make calling on you dear to me, so that
no weariness ever comes over my asking.
19.sharh: What he wants shaped this time is his desire to pray. If he comes to love the asking itself, waiting for an answer need not exhaust it.

translation: Ever-Forgiving One, forgive sins that you know
which have brought me loss and left me impaired.
20.sharh: He leaves the inventory of his offences to God. What he himself can describe is their cost and the damage they have already done.

translation: Overpowering One, subdue an enemy who keeps belittling me
till people see him as lower than a dung beetle.
21.sharh: An enemy has made him feel small. In the angry reversal he imagines, the whole world looks down on that enemy as lower than a dung beetle.

translation: Giver of gifts, give me abundant, ample provision,
and knowledge and understanding joined to action.
22.sharh: The first gift is material abundance. The next two are knowledge and understanding, and he stipulates that both should find their way into what he actually does.

translation: Provider, I am poor. You are the one who sustains me.
Make my provision easy to obtain and send it soon.
23.sharh: The previous verse asked how much might be given. Poverty now lends urgency to two different questions, how hard it will be to obtain and how soon it will come.

translation: Opener, I ask you for a decisive victory, so that
you may bring down my enemies even on the heights.
24.sharh: The opening he seeks is a decisive victory. Elevation gives his adversaries their apparent advantage and also makes their imagined fall visible.

translation: All-Knowing One, grant me knowledge from you that carries me
towards reverence, and shelter me from the band of disputants.
25.sharh: Learning has a direction here, towards a more God-conscious life. The company of habitual disputants offers another use for the same ability to reason.

translation: You who withhold, seize the enemy who comes to trick me.
Strike him with distress, bankruptcy and ruin of mind.
26.sharh: The enemy approaches by stealth. The speaker wants him caught and pictures his undoing in three forms, reaching from outward hardship and loss of money to the mind itself.

translation: You who spread bounty and blessings, extend to me
my livelihood, and let me spend it in the best ways.
27.sharh: Withholding gives way to an open hand. Receiving and spending are assigned to different hands, and his own part is to put the gift to good use.

translation: You who bring low, bring low all enemies of the Reminder
and those who reject the reports of the foremost messenger.
28.sharh: “The Reminder” here means the Quran. The poet puts opposition to it beside rejection of the Prophet's transmitted words, preparing a pair of verses about abasement and elevation.

translation: You who raise up, raise our good name and standing
through our following the Chosen One in word and deed.
29.sharh: He links an honoured name to a particular obligation. To follow someone's tracks, the image in the Arabic, means taking the Prophet as a model in speech as well as action.

translation: You confer honour. For anyone you honour there rise
banners of victory across plain and mountain.
30.sharh: Honour becomes something people can see above them. By planting the imagined banners in both plain and mountain he takes in the whole landscape.

translation: You bring low. Anyone you abase sees
his armies routed and falls into the worst of refuges.
31.sharh: The rising banners of the preceding verse give way to a falling leader. His army breaks first, leaving the man who relied on it to face his own descent.

translation: Hearer of prayer, I call on you in supplication.
You, my Lord, answer everyone who pleads.
32.sharh: He speaks as one petitioner and ends in the company of all petitioners. The repeated word for pleading carries him from his own voice to the assurance on which it depends.

translation: You who see my condition, my sight is gone.
Give me insight so that I may escape error.
33.sharh: The poet says directly that he has lost his sight. Three closely related Arabic words carry him from being seen by God, through his own blindness, to the inward sight he can still ask for.

translation: Before the highest Judge I bring the one
who wronged me and would not heed my reproach.
34.sharh: His attempt at remonstrance has already failed. The language now belongs to a court, with the injured party bringing the matter before a judge above both men.

translation: Our Lord is just. As for whoever comes to wrong me,
seize him with ruin, destruction and disease.
35.sharh: The plaintiff now specifies the punishment he wants. The appeal to divine justice and the injured man's own anger can both be heard in the line.

translation: Be gentle with us in life, Gentle One, and grant
a good ending when our allotted time runs out.
36.sharh: A lifetime of gentle care ends in one moment of particular need. The request for a good ending belongs to everyone included in his “us”.

translation: All-Aware One, give us experience and discernment
with which to go earnestly on, free of sloth.
37.sharh: Experience supplies what a person has learnt, discernment the judgement to use it. Their value is tested in the purposeful movement of the second half.

translation: Forbearing One, grant us forbearance when we see
some slip in one of our brothers.
38.sharh: Forbearance has a concrete occasion, catching a brother in a fault. Calling it “some slip” already practises a little of the restraint he asks for.

translation: You are the Magnificent. Generously magnify our reward
and bestow on us a bounty that will stay.
39.sharh: Magnitude and duration are different good things. He asks for a reward that is great and for favour that will still be there afterwards.

translation: You are the Forgiving. Grant me your forgiveness
for every sin, and give me the greatest gifts.
40.sharh: Earlier he spoke of damage specific sins had done. Here the scope is every sin, and forgiveness clears the way for a further, positive gift.

translation: You who reward gratitude, make me always thankful
for what you have bestowed, and grant my request.
41.sharh: God's appreciation and human gratitude belong to the same word family. He puts acknowledgement of what he has already received before the next request.

translation: Most High, raise my standing in your sight, then
among all people, from the lowly to the great.
42.sharh: The order matters to him. Only after asking for standing with God does he ask for it among people, and the word “then” itself straddles the break.

translation: Great One, make esteem my companion,
and diminish my rival and place him among the lowly.
43.sharh: His opponent is called a qirn, a match for someone in a contest. The verbal contrast makes a wish for distinction into a wish that the equal should cease to be his equal.

translation: Guardian over all things without exception,
bless my efforts and keep me from failure.
44.sharh: The object of protection is unusually specific, his own efforts. He wants blessing in the work as well as protection from a disappointing outcome.

translation: Sustainer, always make our food easy to obtain
from lawful sources, and save us from stinginess.
45.sharh: He needs to eat, but he also cares where the food comes from. The last request looks beyond obtaining it to the danger of refusing to share it.

translation: You are sufficient. Enough for me is to gain your pleasure,
whether I am in sorrow or in delight.
46.sharh: God's pleasure is the measure of what will suffice him. The possessive ending of the Arabic word for “your pleasure” arrives across the break, followed by the two moods through which that judgement holds.

translation: Majestic One, always grant our company
the honour of dignity and keep us from fear.
47.sharh: Majesty is invoked on behalf of his own company. They seek both the dignity that others might recognise and the freedom from fear they would feel for themselves.

translation: Generous giver, we are thirsty.
Give us access to water, a first drink and another.
48.sharh: Two old watering terms make generosity measurable. There is enough for the thirsty to drink on arrival and to come back for a second draught.

translation: You are the Watcher. Grant me your covering over
whatever sin or failing has been mine.
49.sharh: A watcher sees what someone might ordinarily try to conceal. Precisely because concealment from God is impossible, the speaker can only ask God himself to cover the fault.

translation: Answerer of prayer, answer my prayer,
and by your grace keep me from humiliation and shame.
50.sharh: The general assurance that prayers are answered becomes personal. The break runs through the Arabic word for “keep me safe”, holding back for a moment the humiliation and shame he dreads.

translation: You whose bounty is boundless, always broaden our livelihood,
and grant us a dear friend, a helper and protector.
51.sharh: Room to live on is only one kind of abundance. His wish for an intimate friend who will stand by the group names something money alone cannot supply.

translation: Wise One, grant me wisdom and guidance,
and grant a clear victory to cool my burning thirst.
52.sharh: The desire for vindication is a burning thirst that victory might cool. Wisdom and guidance are asked for first, before the heat of his grievance shows itself.

translation: Loving One, grant me love in its fullness
so that I may long for you with all my heart.
53.sharh: Love and longing mark two moments in the same experience. The poet calls the capacity to long wholeheartedly a gain worth asking for in its own right.

translation: Glorious One, honour us through remembering you
in hardship and in ease, without failing or tiring.
54.sharh: Glory is sought in an activity as ordinary and repeatable as remembrance. Two quite different things could interrupt it, inability to continue or simply growing tired of it.

translation: You who raise the dead, send us a clear victory
over those who fight the true faith, and send it soon.
55.sharh: The Arabic verb can mean both raising the dead and sending something forth. The poet draws on that range as he asks that victory be sent to his community.

translation: You witness the deeds of people who transgressed and oppressed
and fought the faith of the best of creatures and messengers.
56.sharh: There is no command in this verse. The speaker lays out his charges before the Witness and identifies the faith by the messenger who brought it.

translation: O Truth, the enemies of the true faith have broken faith
and fought its spread by guile and trickery.
57.sharh: He repeats “truth” for God and for the faith, then gives his opponents a contrary vocabulary of treachery and deceit. His complaint concerns their efforts to prevent that faith from spreading.

translation: Trustee, on you I rely today.
Be my helper and preserve me from error.
58.sharh: The plural community gives way to a solitary “I”. Entrusting his affairs to God means seeking help against opposition and protection from a mistake of his own.

translation: Strong One, strengthen our company today
to strive for the faith in earnest, free of sloth.
59.sharh: The group asks for the strength to exert itself in its religious struggle. “Today” gives the need immediacy, and the enemy named in the second half is its own lethargy.

translation: Firm One, make our company steadfast always.
Make it like a mountain with summits ever high.
60.sharh: Where the previous group was ready to act, this one needs staying power. A mountain with its summits held high gives permanence a visible shape.

translation: Protecting Friend, take us in your care and grant us victory.
Make whoever fights us walk through mud.
61.sharh: After his image of a steadfast mountain, the ground changes under the opponent's feet. Mud makes each forward step uncertain, a physical picture of the frustration the speaker wishes on him.

translation: Praiseworthy One, help us to praise you
in hardship and ease, in safety and in fear.
62.sharh: A person can be prosperous yet frightened, or poor yet safe. The two pairs make his undertaking to give praise wider than a simple contrast between good times and bad.

translation: You keep count of all who have ever opposed guidance.
Make them fall through the deceit they themselves devised.
63.sharh: Each adversary is individually within God's reckoning. The punishment imagined here has a particular symmetry, with a scheme bringing down its own devisers.

translation: Originator, grant us safety and well-being
at home, on journeys and when we move from place to place.
64.sharh: Safety is wanted at three scales, at home, on a journey and in the upheaval of moving from one place to another. The last adds something that simply asking for safe travel would miss.

translation: Restorer, restore to the faith its former strength,
as it was among the first of our forebears.
65.sharh: Restoration gives the petition a direction in time. He looks back to the vigour he ascribes to earlier generations to describe what he would like to see again.

translation: You who revive crumbled remains, bring us to life
through the Chosen One's example in word and deed.
66.sharh: Two forms of life meet. After the literal revival of crumbled bones comes the moral renewal that the speaker seeks through following the Prophet's speech and conduct.

translation: You who give death, let the confession of God's oneness accompany us
when we die, so we may be spared shame.
67.sharh: The profession that there is no god but God becomes a companion at the instant of death. What he wants to take with him here is a form of speech.

translation: Living One, give life to my heart that I may stay
on the safe path wherever I lodge or travel.
68.sharh: Having asked for words to accompany the dying, he turns to a heart that can guide the living. Stopping and setting out are the two rhythms of that life.

translation: My Lord, you are the Sustainer. No one
stands except by the gifts you bestow on him.
69.sharh: The Arabic for sustaining and for standing share a root. The sound ties them together just as the meaning makes one dependent on the other.

translation: You who lack nothing, give every one of us understanding
with which to untie the hardest problems.
70.sharh: Understanding is asked for everyone together. Its test is whether they can undo a difficulty as one might untie a knot that has resisted the hand.

translation: Noble One, grant us a nobility that sets us apart
from those who have joined the ranks of the neglected.
71.sharh: The opposite of distinction is pictured through an old term for camels left untended. He fears belonging to a company that counts for little and has lost its direction.

translation: One God, give us the full confession of your oneness.
Make it our adornment and spare us from going bare.
72.sharh: Belief in divine oneness becomes an ornament one can wear. The answering word for its absence means being bare of jewellery, so both halves belong to one image.

translation: You, our Lord, are one God.
Only someone of unsound judgement consents to give you partners.
73.sharh: The ornament gives way to a statement of belief. In the speaker's judgement, ascribing a partner to the one God is a failure of discernment.

translation: Unique One, you alone create all creatures.
Whoever acknowledges your oneness reaches the utmost hope.
74.sharh: Creation supplies his reason for worshipping one God. The first half speaks of an act that belongs to God alone, the second of what a worshipper can do in response.

translation: You to whom all turn, whoever seeks you wins
every good that embraces what one hopes for.
75.sharh: Al-Samad is the One to whom people turn with their needs. The verb for seeking someone out lets the listener hear that sense through an action rather than a definition.

translation: Powerful One, decree victory for us
over those states that have acted unjustly.
76.sharh: Power and the act of ordaining share a root in Arabic. The poet identifies the states in his prayer by the injustice he ascribes to them and supplies no proper names.

translation: You have full power and are forbearing.
Forgive our sin, you who forgive slips.
77.sharh: The change of subject is sharp. Having asked for power to be exercised against others, the group remembers its own sin and appeals to the restraint of the very One who could punish it.

translation: You who bring forward, always advance our delegation,
and let the favour I hope for be my reliance.
78.sharh: His group appears as a delegation waiting to be received. The change from “our delegation” to “my reliance” makes the speaker personally answerable for where he places his hope.

translation: You who put behind, hold back whoever fights us.
My master, place him among the lowly.
79.sharh: The opponent is the counterpart of the delegation just brought forward. Being put back begins as a matter of position and ends as a loss of standing.

translation: First One, generously grant me a foremost place,
and make loving you sweeter to me than honey.
80.sharh: Standing first can be seen from outside. The taste of honey brings the next wish inward, asking what loving God will actually feel like to the speaker.

translation: Last One, keep our enemies back always
and grant us a victory complete in every respect.
81.sharh: First and Last make a pair of addresses. The speaker turns the sound of “last” into a verb that would set his enemies back, while he asks that his own side's success lack nothing.

translation: Manifest One, make the party of right guidance prevail
over whoever comes to deceive them by malice and fraud.
82.sharh: To “make manifest” can also mean to give someone the upper hand. The open triumph he imagines answers the concealed deceit he attributes to an adversary.

translation: Hidden One, always make my inner self
free of grief, grudges and concealed ill will.
83.sharh: Having complained of deceit in others, he turns his attention within. He names both the grief he suffers himself and the grudges he might bear against someone else.

translation: You are guardian of those who seek your help
against their enemies, early in the day and late.
84.sharh: A declaration takes the place of a request. Early morning and late afternoon mark out a whole day in which those seeking help can turn to their guardian.

translation: Our exalted Lord, guard us always
from every grudge-bearer who lays claim to sound judgement.
85.sharh: This adversary claims to offer sound counsel while harbouring resentment. The danger lies in how readily the claim might disguise the grudge.

translation: From you, Beneficent One, I hope for kindness to enfold me
until tomorrow I come among the finest companies.
86.sharh: “Tomorrow” looks ahead to the life to come. The sign of kindness he hopes for then is the company into which he will be received.

translation: Accepter of repentance, turn to us, accept us and always spare us
harm from evildoers, barefoot or shod.
87.sharh: Turning back and being accepted come before a request for shelter. Barefoot and shod are complementary halves of an old expression that leaves nobody out.

translation: My Lord, you exact retribution. Take my part against
all my enemies. Cast humiliation and folly upon them.
88.sharh: The prayer passes from a statement about divine retribution to an aggrieved person's wish to be avenged. Al-Abdali qualifies retribution by its proper object, someone who merits it.

translation: Pardoning One, pardon my sin. Your bounty is great
towards one who fears you and seeks restored favour.
89.sharh: The man who has just asked for retribution now needs pardon himself. The rare word for the petitioner suggests someone trying to regain favour after giving offence.

translation: Tenderly compassionate to all believers, overlook
the stumbles of a weak servant ashamed of going too far.
90.sharh: Wrongdoing appears as a stumble from which someone needs help to rise. He calls himself weak, yet his shame comes from knowing how far he has overstepped.

translation: Master of all dominion, generously grant my desire
and keep from me the harm of the unjust and foolish.
91.sharh: A sound play matches a harmless human desire with another person's wrongful overreaching. It lets one Arabic root carry both the thing he asks for and the thing he fears.

translation: Lord of majesty and honour, forgive my slips
and always be with me in a grave calamity.
92.sharh: Majesty at the opening is echoed in the Arabic word for a grave event at the close. Between them he asks pardon for his own small slips and companionship in a large calamity.

translation: Just One, give us scales to go with us
when we judge, so justice suffers no defect.
93.sharh: Earlier he appeared as a plaintiff. Now he imagines his community sitting in judgement, where they themselves need a balance that weighs fairly.

translation: Gatherer of people, always bring us together
upon guidance, by following the foremost messenger.
94.sharh: Gathering all people evokes a universal act. The immediate wish is more intimate, to keep a particular community together around a shared practice of following the Prophet.

translation: Self-Sufficient One, in your generosity make us free of need.
Grant us provision like rain pouring down.
95.sharh: God's self-sufficiency becomes a prayer for enough to live without want. The downpour gives that provision weight, movement and abundance one could see.

translation: You enrich all creatures, yet your servant is thirsty.
Let him drink again after his first draught.
96.sharh: The old watering terms return from verse 48. There a whole company approached the water, while here one thirsty servant asks the giver of plenty for a further drink.

translation: Protector, shield a little servant who takes refuge in you
from his enemies' injustice, and bring them quickly to ruin.
97.sharh: The same verb that can mean withholding here means protecting someone. Calling himself a “little servant” makes the harsh wish for his enemies at the end particularly striking.

translation: You who ordain harm, I am afflicted and in need
of your good pleasure. Grant what I ask and hope for.
98.sharh: He begins with harm already suffered, then names approval as his deepest need. The next verse completes the pair by asking what would genuinely benefit him.

translation: You who bring benefit, benefit me with knowledge
with which you adorn me, sparing me the shame of going bare.
99.sharh: Knowledge takes the place of jewellery, recalling his earlier image of belief as an ornament. The benefit he seeks is relief from the disgrace of having nothing with which to adorn himself.

translation: You are light, and my heart is dark and afraid.
Grant me light, and safety that dispels my fear.
100.sharh: The two needs get two answers. Darkness calls for light, while fear requires security, and finding one's way is different from feeling safe enough to take it.

translation: You guide. Grant me lasting guidance
so I may walk without floundering or sinking in mud.
101.sharh: A walker can go wrong through unguided movement or become stuck on the ground itself. The path image gives guidance both a direction to follow and a way past impediments.

translation: Originator of sky and earth, take my hand
and ease my journey on the straightest paths.
102.sharh: The speaker places a single outstretched hand against the scale of sky and earth. Ease alone is insufficient for him unless it carries him along the straightest course.

translation: You alone endure and never pass away. All
besides you meet their end on plain and mountain.
103.sharh: Plain and mountain once carried the verse's banners of victory. Here both are places where creatures perish, giving the same expanse of ground a different meaning.

translation: Heir to the earth and all horizons, generously grant
a good ending when my own time runs out.
104.sharh: Inheritance follows naturally on the passing of all creatures. The poet turns that wide prospect into a request about one death, his own.

translation: Guide of sound judgement, lead me along the path of rectitude
till tomorrow I come dressed in the finest robes.
105.sharh: Today's road leads to tomorrow's clothing. The fine robes picture the condition in which he hopes to arrive in the hereafter, recalling the earlier robes of bodily health.

translation: Patient One, grant me patience at its finest
under calamities wherever I lodge or travel.
106.sharh: This prayer asks how to bear a calamity once it has come. Whether stopped or on the move, he wants a patience whose quality deserves to be called beautiful.

translation: Helper of all creatures, I seek rescue from you alone.
Your help suffices me in place of a household of attendants.
107.sharh: Even the word meaning “other than you” reaches across the verse break. The contrast is between a single source of rescue and all the attendants a person might count on.

translation: You who are near, grant me nearness to you.
I stand at your door and will never turn away.
108.sharh: Nearness becomes a place the listener can picture. The petitioner has reached a door and declares that he has no wish to move away from it.

translation: I have called on you by your most beautiful names. No
hope placed in you fails, One without beginning.
109.sharh: The poet can now speak of the prayer as something accomplished. Calling God one and without beginning takes the listener back to the words with which the work began.

translation: Then blessings, and a greeting of peace with them,
upon the one who brought us the best of faiths,
110.sharh: He resumes the opening blessing and joins to it a greeting of peace. For a moment the Prophet is identified by his message alone, with his name held for the next verse.

translation: Muhammad the Chosen, and all his family,
as long as a camel-driver's song delights his pale camels.
111.sharh: The name completes the blessing begun a verse earlier. Its duration is measured by a continuing human sound, the song with which a driver delights his camels on the road.

2.2.5.head: النُّزُل
2.2.5.meaning: Hospitality prepared for a guest on arrival, hence an honoured welcome.

3.1.4.head: سائِل
3.1.4.meaning: The person who petitions him. The word names the worshipper whose sincerity is described next.

4.1.3-4.head: وَجه الإِلَه
4.1.3-4.meaning: “Seeking God's face” expresses the desire to please God alone.

8.2.4.head: لَجَّ
8.2.4.meaning: Persisted, continued wilfully in a course of action.

9.2.5.head: مُبرِئ
9.2.5.meaning: One who brings about a cure.

10.1.1.head: قُدّوس
10.1.1.meaning: The Most Holy, free from imperfection. The prayer turns from this name to purity of heart.

11.2.7.head: خَطَل
11.2.7.meaning: Unsound judgement or foolish, ill-considered speech.

12.1.2.head: مُؤمِن
12.1.2.meaning: Giver of security, the sense of the name on which this prayer turns.

13.1.2.head: مُهَيمِن
13.1.2.meaning: The watchful guardian who keeps those in his care in view.

14.2.4.head: الأَبَد
14.2.4.meaning: Ages extending into the future, the plural of the word for an unending span.

15.2.5.head: الأَصيل
15.2.5.meaning: Late afternoons or evenings, paired here with the beginning of the day.

16.2.5.head: السُّفُل
16.2.5.meaning: The lower reaches, here a fall from the standing a proud person claims.

18.1.4.head: بُرء
18.1.4.meaning: Recovery from illness. Its consonants echo the divine name Bari', the Originator.

18.2.4.head: سابِغ
18.2.4.meaning: Ample, covering the whole body, of a garment.

19.2.2.head: اِعتَرى
19.2.2.meaning: To come over or befall someone.

21.2.7.head: الجُعَل
21.2.7.meaning: A dung beetle, the lowly creature in the poet's comparison.

22.1.6.head: غَدَق
22.1.6.meaning: Abundant, originally said of plentiful water.

24.2.1.head: أَردى
24.2.1.meaning: To bring down or bring to ruin.

25.2.5.head: عُصبَة
25.2.5.meaning: A band of people. The collected edition prints usayya and records usba from Sawt al-Umma in its margin. The recitation and al-Abdali give the latter.

26.1.6.head: خَتَلَ
26.1.6.meaning: To approach by stealth and take someone unawares.

26.2.4.head: الخَبَل
26.2.4.meaning: Derangement or loss of sound judgement.

28.1.5.head: الذِّكر
28.1.5.meaning: The Reminder, here the Quran, paired with transmitted reports of the Prophet.

29.2.1.head: قَفو
29.2.1.meaning: Following in someone's tracks, hence taking that person as a model.

31.2.5.head: مُدَّخَل
31.2.5.meaning: A place entered or resorted to, here the sorry refuge of someone put to flight.

32.1.3.head: الدُّعاء
32.1.3.meaning: Prayer or supplication. The usual final hamza drops in this metrical form.

33.1.2.head: بَصير
33.1.2.meaning: One who sees and knows his condition. The recording uses the accusative basiran where the collected edition omits the accusative alif.

34.2.6.head: عَذل
34.2.6.meaning: Reproach, an attempt to bring a wrongdoer to his senses.

35.2.2.head: قَصم
35.2.2.meaning: A shattering blow, ruin that breaks something's strength.

36.2.4.head: اِنقِضاء
36.2.4.meaning: The coming to an end. The final hamza of the usual form is shortened in verse.

37.1.6.head: حِجى
37.1.6.meaning: Discernment, the faculty for judging a course of action.

41.2.5.head: سُؤل
41.2.5.meaning: The thing prayed for, the object of a request.

43.2.2.head: القِرن
43.2.2.meaning: An opponent matched with another in strength.

45.1.4.head: قوت
45.1.4.meaning: The food that keeps a person alive from day to day.

46.2.8.head: جَذَل
46.2.8.meaning: Delight, the emotional opposite of the sorrow just named.

48.2.2.head: الوِرد
48.2.2.meaning: Access to a watering place, or one's turn to drink there.

48.2.4.head: نَهَل
48.2.4.meaning: The first draught after reaching water.

48.2.6.head: عَلَل
48.2.6.meaning: A return draught after the first drink.

49.1.4.head: سِتر
49.1.4.meaning: A covering that spares a person exposure for a fault.

51.2.3.head: خِلّ
51.2.3.meaning: An intimate friend, someone bound to another by deep affection.

52.2.5.head: غُلَل
52.2.5.meaning: Burning thirsts, here the longings that victory would soothe.

54.2.4.head: عَجز
54.2.4.meaning: Incapacity. It differs from losing the desire to continue while still able.

55.1.2.head: باعِث
55.1.2.meaning: Raiser of the dead. The following verb from the same root means to send forth.

56.1.5.head: طَغى
56.1.5.meaning: They overstepped the bounds of right conduct.

57.1.5.head: الحَقّ
57.1.5.meaning: Truth, here qualifying the faith. The collected edition has “faith of truth” and al-Abdali's text has “faith of God”.

58.2.5.head: الخَطَل
58.2.5.meaning: An error of speech or judgement. Al-Abdali's text here has khalal, a fault or deficiency.

59.1.5.head: زُمرَة
59.1.5.meaning: The company or body of people to which the speaker belongs.

60.2.2.head: الطَّود
60.2.2.meaning: A great mountain, called up for both its height and its steadiness.

61.2.6.head: الوَحَل
61.2.6.meaning: Soft mud in which feet sink and progress slows.

63.2.1.head: أَوقِع
63.2.1.meaning: Bring them down through their own plotting. The collected edition marks a light emphatic nun before “them”. Al-Abdali gives the heavier, doubled ending.

63.2.5.head: دَخَل
63.2.5.meaning: A hidden defect or deceit concealed beneath an outward appearance.

64.2.5.head: نُقلَة
64.2.5.meaning: Moves or changes of residence, beyond a journey made and returned from.

66.1.3.head: الرُّفات
66.1.3.meaning: Crumbled remains, especially bones. Both printed texts spell the ending with ta marbuta. The Quranic word for them ends in ordinary t.

67.1.4.head: التَّهليل
67.1.4.meaning: Tahlil, the profession “There is no god but God.”

68.2.4-5.head: حِلّ ومُرتَحَل
68.2.4-5.meaning: “My lodging and my departure”, a pair covering life at rest and on the move.

70.2.6.head: عُضلَة
70.2.6.meaning: Intractable problems that defy a ready solution.

71.2.2.head: الأُلى
71.2.2.meaning: Those who, an older relative pronoun.

71.2.7.head: الهَمَل
71.2.7.meaning: Those left untended. Its older use includes camels without a herdsman.

72.2.5.head: العَطَل
72.2.5.meaning: Going unadorned, especially having no jewellery at the neck or wrist.

73.2.3.head: الشِّرك
73.2.3.meaning: Shirk, ascribing a partner to God in worship.

75.1.3.head: صَمَد
75.1.3.meaning: Al-Samad, the One to whom all turn for their needs. The following verb expresses that movement.

76.2.3.head: بَغى
76.2.3.meaning: They acted unjustly or encroached on the rights of others.

78.1.4.head: وَفد
78.1.4.meaning: A delegation arriving for an audience.

78.2.5.head: مُتَّكَل
78.2.5.meaning: That on which I can rely or lean.

81.1.3.head: أَخِّر
81.1.3.meaning: Put back or delay. A light emphatic nun reinforces the entreaty.

82.1.3.head: أَظهِر
82.1.3.meaning: Give the upper hand. With the preposition “over”, the verb means to prevail.

83.2.5.head: دَغَل
83.2.5.meaning: An admixture of concealed ill will or corruption.

85.2.4.head: إِحنَة
85.2.4.meaning: Old resentments kept in the heart.

85.2.6.head: مُنتَحِل
85.2.6.meaning: Someone falsely claiming good judgement as his own.

86.2.6.head: ثُلَّة
86.2.6.meaning: Companies or multitudes of people, here companions in the life to come.

87.2.5-6.head: حافٍ ومُنتَعِل
87.2.5-6.meaning: “Barefoot and shod”, a paired expression covering everybody.

88.2.5.head: هَبَل
88.2.5.meaning: Loss of judgement or bewilderment in the speaker's imprecation.

89.2.4.head: مُستَعتِب
89.2.4.meaning: Someone seeking reconciliation and the return of favour.

90.1.5.head: أَقِل
90.1.5.meaning: Overlook a stumble and help the one who fell to recover.

90.2.1.head: عِثار
90.2.1.meaning: A stumble of the foot, figuratively a lapse into wrongdoing.

91.1.6.head: بُغيَة
91.1.6.meaning: My desire or goal. The same root supplies a word for wrongful overreaching in the next half.

92.2.6.head: جَلَل
92.2.6.meaning: Grave or momentous, qualifying the calamity.

93.1.5.head: القِسطاس
93.1.5.meaning: An accurate balance, here the standard by which a judgement can be fair.

94.1.5.head: شَمل
94.1.5.meaning: The unity of a group, or its members as a whole.

95.2.4-5.head: الوابِل الهَطِل
95.2.4-5.meaning: “A heavy downpour”, rain falling copiously and steadily.

96.2.2.head: عَلَل
96.2.2.meaning: A second drink after the first, here an image of receiving more after immediate need has been met.

97.1.4.head: عُبَيد
97.1.4.meaning: A little servant. The diminutive makes the speaker seem especially small and dependent.

98.2.4.head: سُؤل
98.2.4.meaning: The object of a petition, what the person hopes to be granted.

99.2.2.head: زَيَّنَ
99.2.2.meaning: You adorn me. Both printed witnesses point the doubled verb zayyana, which supplies the syllables required by the metre.

99.2.4.head: وَصمَة
99.2.4.meaning: A blemish, a mark of disgrace.

100.1.5.head: وَهِل
100.1.5.meaning: Alarmed or fearful, said of the heart.

101.2.4.head: خَبط
101.2.4.meaning: Blundering movement without a clear course.

102.1.3.head: السَّماء
102.1.3.meaning: The sky, in the shortened poetic form sama.

103.2.3.head: الفَناء
103.2.3.meaning: Passing away, in a metrical form which shortens the usual final syllable.

104.1.4.head: أُفُق
104.1.4.meaning: Horizons, the reaches of the earth as far as one can see.

105.2.6.head: حُلَّة
105.2.6.meaning: Fine garments or robes used for adornment.

107.2.7.head: خَوَل
107.2.7.meaning: A person's household attendants and dependants.

108.2.7.head: حِوَل
108.2.7.meaning: A change of place, here the act of turning away from the door.

111.2.3.head: العيس
111.2.3.meaning: Light-coloured camels whose pale coats have a reddish tinge.

111.2.4.head: حادٍ
111.2.4.meaning: A camel-driver singing the rhythmic chant that accompanies the herd on its way.

2.2.3.head: ذَوو
2.2.3.meaning: Possessors of honour and welcome. The plural describes the Prophet's family. Al-Abdali's running text has the singular dhu.

11.1.3.head: سَلامَة
11.1.3.meaning: Kinds of safety. Both editions and the studio card have the plural. The sung vowel could also be heard as the singular salama.

18.2.3.meaning: “Of it”, referring to recovery. This makes health the very fabric of his clothing. Al-Abdali's running text gives “from you”.

34.2.4.head: أَصغى
34.2.4.meaning: To listen attentively. Arabic shortens the ending after lam, even when the reciter sustains it.

85.1.3.head: المُتَعالي
85.1.3.meaning: The Exalted, above any imperfection. The performance gives the full ending where both printed texts omit the final ya.

96.2.1.head: اِسقِ
96.2.1.meaning: Give him a drink. The two Arabic verb forms saqa and asqa both express giving water here.

109.2.3.head: الرَّجاء
109.2.3.meaning: Hope of receiving good. The poetic form shortens the ordinary ending of raja'.
